# Glossary {.unnumbered}

```{=latex}
\begingroup\small
```

One plain sentence for each term, and the chapter where it's explained properly.

Act, review, escalate
: The three zones of a decision policy: handle it automatically, send it to a person, or raise it urgently (Chapter 14).

Agent
: A program that uses a model to observe, decide and act in a loop, calling tools along the way (Chapter 7).

Attention
: A way for each word in a sequence to look at the others and decide which ones matter for its meaning (Chapter 5).

Audit (random)
: Sending a random share of automatically handled cases to a person, so that mistakes the system is sure about still get seen (Chapter 14).

AUC
: The chance that a model gives a randomly chosen real case a higher score than a randomly chosen harmless one; it measures ranking, not calibration (Chapter 3).

Base rate
: How common something is before you look at any evidence, like the share of alerts that are real threats (Chapter 2).

Brier score
: The average squared gap between a predicted probability and what happened; lower is better (Chapters 2 and 3).

Calibration
: A model is calibrated when the things it calls 70% likely happen about 70% of the time (Chapter 3).

Capacity
: How many cases the people in the loop can handle in a day; a policy that ignores it isn't a policy (Chapter 14).

Cassette
: A file of recorded requests and responses that a test can replay without calling the real API (Chapter 16).

CISO
: Chief information security officer: the person in charge of an organisation's security (Chapter 18).

Choice
: A typed question with a set of named options; the answer is a probability for each option, adding up to 1 (Chapter 10).

Confidence
: In a Jev `choice` or `score` answer, a number from 0 to 1 computed from the shape of the probabilities: high when they're concentrated on one option, low when they're spread out. It isn't simply the top probability (TypeSafe's quick-start shows 0.78 beside 0.85). The book's mock uses the top probability as a stand-in (Chapter 9).

Context window
: The amount of text an LLM can read at once (Chapter 7).

Cost line
: The probability above which acting is cheaper than not acting, set by what each kind of mistake costs (Chapter 4).

Decision layer
: The part of a system that turns probabilities into actions: typed questions, calibration, lines, rules and fail-safes (Part IV).

Decision record
: The logged account of one decision: what was seen, what the model said, what the policy did, which version decided and why (Chapter 21).

Drift
: A change in the world, or in the data, that makes a model's probabilities less accurate than when they were checked (Chapter 14).

DLP (data loss prevention)
: Security tools that warn when company data may be leaving the organisation, such as a large file sent to a personal email address (Chapter 3).

ECE (expected calibration error)
: The average gap between what a model said and what happened, across groups of similar predictions (Chapter 3).

Elasticity
: How much more of something people use when its price falls (Chapter 12).

Embedding
: A list of numbers that places a word, sentence or item in a space where similar things sit close together (Chapter 5).

Epoch
: One full pass of training over all the training examples (Chapter 5).

Escape option
: The "other", "none" or "not enough information" option that gives cases fitting nowhere somewhere to go (Chapter 10).

Extract, then decide
: A pattern in which an LLM turns messy input into fields and a decision model decides on those fields (Chapter 15).

F1
: One score that balances how many flagged cases are real and how many real cases get flagged; it measures ranking and labelling, not calibration (Chapter 3).

Fail-safe
: The decided meaning of a failure, such as "if the call fails, send the case to review" (Chapters 14 and 21).

Fine-tuning
: Further training of an existing model on examples from one task (Chapter 5).

Gradient descent
: Improving a model step by step by nudging its numbers in the direction that reduces the loss (Chapter 2).

Guardrail gate
: A typed check on trusted facts that runs before an agent's action is allowed to happen (Chapter 15).

Hallucination
: An LLM stating something fluent and false (Chapter 6).

Hybrid agent
: An agent in which a decision model answers the small decisions and an LLM only writes (Chapter 17).

Isotonic regression
: A calibration method that learns any increasing mapping from scores to probabilities; flexible, but needs more data than Platt scaling (Chapter 3).

Jevons paradox
: When making something more efficient to use makes people use more of it in total, not less (Chapter 12).

JSON mode
: An LLM setting that makes its output valid JSON, though not necessarily correct JSON (Chapter 6).

Label
: The known right answer for an example, used to train or test a model (Chapter 1).

LLM (large language model)
: A model trained to predict the next piece of text, which lets it read and write almost anything (Chapter 6).

LLM-as-judge
: Using an LLM to rate or check an output, often on a numbered scale (Chapter 13).

Log loss
: A score that punishes confident wrong answers heavily; a proper scoring rule (Chapter 2).

Logistic regression
: A model that adds up weighted evidence and passes the total through an S-curve to get a probability (Chapter 2).

Loss
: A number that measures how wrong a model is on some examples; training tries to make it smaller (Chapter 2).

Mock
: A stand-in for a real service that answers in the same shape; this book's is `jev-mock-synthetic` (Chapter 16).

Noul
: TypeSafe's name for a yes-or-no question; the answer is the probability of yes (Chapter 10).

Observe, Decide, Act
: The loop an agent runs: read something, choose what to do, do it, repeat (Chapter 7).

Ordinal
: Having a meaningful order, like severity levels; an ordinal model keeps that order in its probabilities (Chapter 20).

Overconfidence
: Probabilities that are more extreme than the evidence justifies; common in large models and in overtrained small ones (Chapter 5).

Overfitting
: Learning the training examples so closely that performance on new examples gets worse (Chapter 2).

Platt scaling
: A calibration method that fits an S-curve mapping a model's scores to calibrated probabilities (Chapter 3).

Policy
: The rules that turn a probability into an action, usually as lines between zones (Chapter 14).

Prior shift
: A change in the base rate between where a model was calibrated and where it's used; correctable if the new base rate is known (Chapter 11).

Prompt injection
: Text planted in an input that tries to make a model follow the attacker's instructions (Chapter 7).

Proper scoring rule
: A way of scoring predictions under which reporting your honest probability gives the best average score (Chapter 2).

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
: Giving an LLM relevant documents, found by search, before it answers (Chapter 7).

Reliability diagram
: A chart of what a model said against what happened; a calibrated model sits on the diagonal (Chapter 3).

RLCD
: TypeSafe's name for reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions, which it says trains Jev; details unpublished (Chapter 9).

RLHF
: Reinforcement learning from human feedback, which trains an LLM towards answers people prefer (Chapter 5).

Router
: A pattern that sends each case to a destination with a choice question, falling back to a person when unsure (Chapter 15).

Score
: A typed question with ordered levels; the answer is a probability for each level and an expected level (Chapter 10).

Shadow mode
: Running a new system or version beside the current one, recording what it would do without letting it act (Chapters 18 and 21).

SIEM (security information and event management)
: The tool that collects a company's logs and raises security alerts; Kestrel's alerts come from one (Chapter 13).

Softmax
: The function that turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1 (Chapters 5 and 10).

State
: What a decision model reads: the situation, as text or structured fields (Chapter 9).

Structured output
: An LLM answer constrained to a schema, such as JSON with named fields (Chapter 6).

System 1, System 2
: Kahneman's names for fast, automatic thinking and slow, deliberate thinking (Chapter 8).

System One model
: TypeSafe's term for a model that answers typed questions with probabilities in one fast pass, without writing text (Chapter 8).

Temperature (calibration)
: One number that softens or sharpens every probability a model gives, fitted on held-out data (Chapter 3).

Temperature (sampling)
: A setting that makes an LLM's choice of next token more or less random (Chapter 6).

Three-zone policy
: A policy with two lines, splitting cases into act, review and escalate (Chapter 14).

Token
: A piece of text, often part of a word, that an LLM reads and writes one at a time (Chapter 6).

Trace
: The step-by-step record of what an agent observed, decided and did (Chapter 17).

Transformer
: The network design built from attention layers that underlies modern LLMs (Chapter 5).

Transport
: The lowest layer of an HTTP client, which sends a finished request and returns a response; the book's mock is one (Chapter 16).

Typed question
: A question whose answer has a fixed shape: a noul, a choice or a score (Chapter 10).

Vendor-reported
: A claim made by the company selling the product, not independently checked (Chapter 9).
